A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same neural-operator stress-testing study across five PDE families. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendix A are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial revision.

before.justification: V1 reports original experiments involving 1,000 trained models, with stress-test results, spectral diagnostics, and degradation statistics in Appendix A.

after.justification: V4 reports original experiments involving 750 trained models across three architectures and five PDE families, with results in Figures 1–4 and Appendix A.

M1.justification: Both versions retain the same post-training stress-testing framework, parameter inputs, and worst-case stress-to-baseline error ratio. V4 expands the evaluated architectures without introducing a new learning algorithm or stress-testing component.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate nonlinear Schrödinger, Poisson, 2D Navier–Stokes, Black–Scholes, and Kuramoto–Sivashinsky problems with the same applicable stress scenarios. Kuramoto–Sivashinsky remains limited to rollout and perturbation tests; additional architectures do not introduce new task coverage.

E2.justification: V1 primarily reports FNO results and describes only a limited qualitative DeepONet comparison. V4 evaluates FNO, a DeepONet-style model, and newly added CNO throughout the five PDE families, with all three participating in every applicable comparison in Appendix A.

E3.justification: The core stress procedures and degradation metric remain unchanged. The stated FNO configuration changes from 16 Fourier modes per dimension in v1 to 12×12 modes in 2D in v4, retaining 16 in 1D. V4 also specifies common data-generation and stress-grid controls across architectures; most additional training settings are disclosures rather than established changes to retained experiments.

E4.justification: V1's nonlinear Schrödinger and Navier–Stokes spectral-error analyses, shown in Figures 3 and 6, disappear from v4, together with detailed qualitative rollout observations. V4 instead substantially expands comparative robustness analysis, testing shared versus architecture-specific sensitivities and contrasting baseline rankings with degradation rankings.

E5.justification: The reported ensemble changes from 200 independent models per PDE, totaling 1,000, to 50 per architecture–PDE pair, totaling 750. This reduces FNO replication fourfold while extending replication to the other architectures. Mean, standard deviation, and 95% confidence-interval reporting persist, although v4 omits v1's explicit normal-approximation formula.

E6.justification: Appendix A adds comprehensive DeepONet and CNO results and revises FNO statistics; for example, Navier–Stokes rollout degradation changes from 3.524 to 3.296. New Black–Scholes payoff-shift results report 2.338 for DeepONet and 12.239 for CNO, establishing architecture-dependent differences. Figure 1 also adds baseline-error comparisons. Changed ensembles and configurations prevent interpreting the FNO revisions as same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: V1 explicitly states the governing equations for all five PDEs in the Introduction; v4 removes these mathematical specifications while retaining verbal descriptions. The formal degradation-factor definition is unchanged, and neither version presents theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions, and conclusion shift from an FNO-centered failure-mode atlas emphasizing spectral bias and perturbation stability to a systematic three-architecture evaluation framework. The central new claim is that baseline accuracy does not predict degradation rankings, with shared, architecture-dependent, and PDE-specific failures becoming explicit main contributions.

C2.justification: V1's extensive explanations involving spectral limitations, implicit smoothing, and damping of chaotic dynamics are largely removed. V4 emphasizes architecture-dependent robustness and conditional generalization, and adds substantive qualifications about comparison fairness and limited PDE coverage. Its Poisson interpretation also shifts from severe boundary failure to resolution and perturbation sensitivity, consistent with the appendix tables.

D1.justification: V4 Section 3.4 newly specifies training sample counts, grids, batch sizes, optimization budgets, Adam learning rate, architecture widths and depths, coordinate channels, and evaluation sample counts. Hardware disclosure expands to CPU, RAM, and GPU specifications. Some earlier loss, early-stopping, and stress-test details are omitted; the stated code repository remains unchanged.

R1.justification: V4 adds a substantial Related Work section and four cited works covering physics-informed machine learning, PINO, CNO, and boundary-indexed operator families. It develops new positioning around conditional generalization and a common robustness-evaluation framework, while retaining v1's six references.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, results, discussion, and conclusion are extensively rewritten and condensed around architectural comparisons. V4 adds Related Work and Experimental Setup sections, groups PDE discussions, moves references before the appendix, and revises the title and affiliation presentation.

P2.justification: V4 redesigns the overview heatmap around architectures and adds a baseline-error panel. Five individual FNO bar charts become grouped architecture comparisons in Figures 2–4, the two spectral plots disappear, and appendix tables gain architecture groups. Parameter-shift results omitted from individual bar panels remain in the overview and tables.

improvement.justification: The systematic architecture comparisons and explicit experimental setup make v4 more informative and reproducible. Its Poisson discussion also resolves v1's mismatch between claims of order-of-magnitude boundary degradation and Table 1's mean of 1.503. The net gain is limited by reduced replication and removal of the spectral evidence that v4 still promises in its abstract and methodology.
